questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presented with fatigue, subjective fever and chills, and poor appetite. He had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and CKD stage 4. He had no known drug allergies. On examination he was found to have a new diastolic murmur. He was started empirically on vancomycin. Investigations: 4/4 blood cultures positive for fully sensitive Enterococcus faecalis Echocardiogram: a 5 mm vegetation of the aortic valve Creatinine clearance 15 mL/min
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone For patients with enterococcal endocarditis with susceptible strains the preferred treatment regimens include ampicillin or penicillin G as these are rapidly cidal agents. For patients with normal renal function these agents should be combined with 2 weeks of aminoglycoside such as gentamicin. In patients with contraindications to aminoglycosides, an alternate regimen of ampicillin and ceftriaxone should be used. Linezolid and daptomycin should be reserved for patients with resistant enterococci not amenable to treatment with rapidly cidal beta-lactams. Vancomycin should be reserved for patients with penicillin-resistant enterococci, and beta-lactams should be used whenever possible. In this patient with a very limited creatinine clearance, vancomycin should also be avoided to prevent further damage to his renal function.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q16

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman was admitted with tachycardia and fever. She had a history of colon cancer, diabetes mellitus, acute on chronic kidney disease, and depression. She was taking citalopram and had a severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis). Investigations: Creatinine 2.9 mg/dL (baseline SCr 1.8 mg/dL) Total white cell count 16.2 ×109/L CXR normal Transthoracic echocardiogram – no evidence of endocarditis 3 sets of blood cultures positive for Enterococcus faecalis: ampicillin: sensitive vancomycin: sensitive daptomycin: sensitive linezolid: sensitive high-level gentamicin resistance: present high-level streptomycin resistance: results pending
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Daptomycin Quinupristin/dalfopristin is not active against E. faecalis . While telavancin is active against vancomycin-susceptible enterococci, the patient has AKI/CKD, which makes this agent undesirable from a safety standpoint. While the strain is ampicillin-susceptible, the patient has a severe penicillin allergy, which precludes ampicillin. Linezolid should be avoided for routine use in combination with selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors. Daptomycin is active against this strain of Enterococcus faecalis, and there is no evidence of pulmonary involvement based on lack of pulmonary/ respiratory symptoms and negative chest X-ray.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q2

questions.question: [image-based question: PFGE (VRE), 9 lanes shown]

parts.text: Interpret 9 lanes on a PFGE
What is a reservoir for this organism besides GI colonization?
What is the most common mechanism of resistance?

questions.model_answer: a) PFGE interpretation: lanes with identical/near-identical banding patterns (≤3 band differences) represent the same/closely related outbreak strain, indicating clonal spread (nosocomial transmission); distinct banding patterns indicate genetically unrelated isolates (polyclonal, sporadic acquisition). b) Reservoir besides GI colonization: environmental surfaces/hospital equipment contamination (VRE survives long periods on surfaces) - also skin colonization and contaminated healthcare worker hands. c) Most common resistance mechanism: acquisition of the vanA gene cluster (plasmid-mediated), altering the D-Ala-D-Ala peptidoglycan precursor target to D-Ala-D-Lac, reducing vancomycin binding affinity.

questions.question: 16. Guy has an Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis. Susceptibility testing shows it is susceptible to ampicillin and vancomycin, but highly resistant to gentamicin and streptomycin.

parts.text: Why does the laboratory report only high level susceptibility?
b) What therapeutic consequence does high-level aminoglycoside resistance have?
c) What is the mechanism of high level aminoglycoside resistance in Enterococci?

cohort_answer.text: Only high-level resistance reported: Don't report low-level resistance since all enterococci have intrinsic low-level resistance to aminoglycosides; loss of synergism with beta lactams/vanco if high-level AG resistance present. Therapeutic consequence: Can no longer use AG for synergy with beta-lactam/vanco against enterococcus, if used will lead to clinical failure/higher relapse. Mechanism: AG-modifying enzymes (N-acetylation, O-nucleotidylation, O-phosphorylation) alter the drug so it can no longer bind the 30s ribosome subunit.

questions.question: Endocarditis to E. faecalis. Sensitive to Ampi, Vanco, Genta (HN), Strepto (HN)

parts.text: Why test high-level resistance to Genta?
What is the high-level resistance mechanism at Genta?
Why is Streptomycin less preferable than Genta in synergistic treatment?

cohort_answer.text:
Why test HLR to Genta: Synergistic activity between cell wall active agents and aminoglycoside is not possible in the setting of high level resistance to Gentamicin. All have low level resistance.
High-level resistance mechanism: Aminoglycoside modifying enzymes – enzyme inactivation
Why Streptomycin less preferable: AHA guidelines: Advantage: less nephrotoxic than gentamicin. Disadvantage: no published studies comparing the efficacy of regimens containing streptomycin or gentamicin; lack of familiarity among clinicians with streptomycin; higher risk of ototoxicity, which may not be reversible; drug availability limitations; most laboratories do not routinely perform serum streptomycin assays; may not have access to a clinical pharmacist to assist in dosing adjustments.

questions.question: 70yo M with recent bioprosthetic aortic valve insertion with E faecalis in 4/4 blood cultures over 48 hours. Susceptible to ampicillin but high level resistance to both gentamicin and streptomycin.

parts.text: What is a diagnostic test you need to do and how would it change management?
Two micro bench characteristics of E faecalis
What is most common reason for aminoglycoside resistance and how is it acquired
What is your antibiotic regimen including duration

questions.model_answer:
a) Diagnostic test: confirm high-level aminoglycoside resistance (HLAR) testing to both gentamicin and streptomycin (already done here) - this determines that aminoglycoside synergy is not achievable, changing management to a dual beta-lactam regimen (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone) instead of ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside.
b) Two bench characteristics of E. faecalis: (1) catalase-negative, gram-positive cocci in chains/pairs (2) growth in bile-esculin agar and in 6.5% NaCl broth (PYR test positive).
c) Most common cause of aminoglycoside resistance in enterococci: production of an aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme (most commonly the bifunctional AAC(6')-APH(2'') enzyme), acquired via plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer.
d) Antibiotic regimen: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual beta-lactam synergistic therapy) for a total of 6 weeks, given HLAR precludes aminoglycoside synergy.

questions.question: Pan susceptible Enterococcus spp.. Why do you test for HLR and what is the mechanism of AG R?

parts.text: Pan susceptible Enterococcus spp.. Why do you test for HLR and what is the mechanism of AG R?

cohort_answer.text: E. faecalis w/ AMG - bi functional aminoglycoside modifying enzyme - APH2 (HLR to gent); HLR to streptomycin can be due to mutations in the 30S ribosomal subunit and to the presence of a streptomycin adenylyltransferase.

parts.text: Explain HLAR, could you use streptomycin if gentamicin was not available?

cohort_answer.text: HLAR mediated by AME (aminoglycoside modifying enzymes) - enzymatic target modification methylating the 30S subunit of ribosome; often on mobile genetic elements (plasmids, transposons), e.g. aac(6')-aph(2"). Streptomycin: HLR to SM can be due to ribosome alteration mutations in 30S ribosomal subunit - must evaluate for HLR separately for both gentamicin and streptomycin. E. faecium has natural resistance to tobramycin but NOT gentamicin. Use of aminoglycosides in IE varies by organism/valve type per detailed regimens (native valve GVS, prosthetic valve, SA prosthetic valve IE, enterococci, GNB IE) - can use streptomycin 15mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses instead of gentamicin, less nephrotoxicity but more ototoxicity, do not use in CrCl<50

questions.question: 20. Explain HLAR, could you use streptomycin if gentamicin was not available?

parts.text: Explain HLAR, could you use streptomycin if gentamicin was not available?

cohort_answer.text: HLAR: mediated by AME (aminoglycoside modifying enzymes) - enzymatic target modification by methylating the 30S ribosomal subunit; high level resistance commonly found on mobile genetic elements (plasmids/transposons), e.g. aac(6')-aph(2''). Streptomycin: HLR to SM can be due to ribosome alteration mutations in the 30S subunit - must evaluate for HLR to both gentamicin and streptomycin in all severe enterococcal infections since mechanisms differ. E. faecium has natural resistance to tobramycin but NOT gentamicin. When to use aminoglycosides in IE: Native valve GVS/S gallolyticus/Abiotrophia/Granulicatella added to beta-lactam as synergy to reduce to 2 weeks in highly sensitive organisms, or first 2 weeks in relatively/highly pen resistant organisms combined with Pen G or CRO. Prosthetic valve GVS/S gallolyticus: first 2 weeks in combination with 6-week PenG/CRO for highly susceptible; for pen-resistant, use 6 weeks with PenG/CRO. Native valve IE by group B/C/G strep: add genta first 2 weeks (total 4-6 weeks). SA prosthetic valve IE: initial 2 weeks genta 3mg/kg/d divided 2-3 doses with cloxacillin+rifampin+early surgery. Enterococci native/prosthetic valve IE: total 4-6 weeks with ampicillin, genta trough <1ug/ml. GNB native/prosthetic valve IE: beta-lactam+aminoglycoside for 6 weeks. Can use streptomycin 15mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses instead of gentamicin (less nephrotoxicity, more ototoxicity, avoid if CrCl<50).

questions.question: E faecalis bacteremia with a prosthetic valve 3 weeks ago. It has HLAR to gent and strepto.

parts.text: What test is required next which will impact treatment?
What treatment regimen and duration?
What's the most common enterococcus resistance to AG and how is it acquired?
Two bench biochemicals for identification

questions.model_answer: a) Next test: repeat/confirm high-level aminoglycoside resistance testing to both gentamicin AND streptomycin specifically (since HLAR to one does not preclude synergy with the other) - this determines whether an aminoglycoside can still be used synergistically. b) Treatment regimen/duration: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual β-lactam synergy, avoids aminoglycoside toxicity) for 6 weeks (prosthetic valve endocarditis); if not HLAR to streptomycin, ampicillin plus streptomycin is an alternative. c) Most common enterococcal aminoglycoside resistance: bifunctional enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia (aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme) conferring high-level resistance to gentamicin (and most aminoglycosides except streptomycin); acquired via plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer/conjugation. d) Two bench biochemical tests for identification: (1) Pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) test - positive in Enterococcus. (2) Growth in 6.5% NaCl broth and bile-esculin hydrolysis (positive for Enterococcus, distinguishes from Streptococcus).

(2) Bile-esculin hydrolysis plus growth in 6.5% NaCl - both positive in Enterococcus, distinguishing from streptococci. b) High-level aminoglycoside resistance mechanism: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia, plasmid-mediated (horizontally transferable), confers resistance to gentamicin (and most aminoglycosides, sparing streptomycin which has a different mechanism). c) Therapy and duration: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual β-lactam synergy) for 6 weeks given prosthetic valve endocarditis.

questions.question: 70M have AVR 3 weeks ago, now fevers/chills. Blood cultures 4/4 Enterococcus faecalis. Susceptible to ampicillin but high-level resistance to gentamicin

parts.text: What is one investigation that you would want to do, and why?

What is the most common mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance, and how is it transmitted between bacteria?
What is your recommended management? (2 points)

questions.model_answer: a) Investigation: transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) - higher sensitivity than TTE for detecting prosthetic valve vegetations/abscess in suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis. b) Two rapid microbiologic identification tests: (1) Pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) test. (2) Bile-esculin hydrolysis with growth in 6.5% NaCl broth. c) Most common aminoglycoside resistance mechanism: bifunctional enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia (aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme), transmitted via plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer (conjugation) between bacteria. d) Recommended management (2 points): (1) Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual β-lactam synergistic therapy, avoiding aminoglycoside given HLR to gentamicin) - note streptomycin susceptibility should still be checked as an alternative synergy option. (2) Total duration of 6 weeks IV therapy for prosthetic valve endocarditis; surgical consultation given prosthetic valve involvement.

questions.question: You see a 15 year-old female patient with several weeks of fever, malaise, and weight loss. Blood cultures are positive for Enterococcus faecalis. Echocardiogram demonstrates a 1.2 cm vegetation on the mitral valve. The E. faecalis isolate is susceptible to ampicillin and aminoglycosides. She is started on ampicillin and gentamicin for 6 weeks.

parts.text: List THREE tests that should be monitored in patients on gentamicin.
List TWO symptoms/signs that may suggest gentamicin toxicity.
List TWO specific cells that are affected in gentamicin toxicity.
Name ONE non-biochemical test that may be used to identify gentamicin toxicity.
After starting gentamicin, the patient develops confusion and muscle weakness. What is the most likely cause and what is the treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Three tests to monitor on gentamicin: (1) serum creatinine/renal function (2) gentamicin peak and trough serum levels (3) baseline and periodic audiometry (hearing assessment).
b) Two symptoms/signs suggesting toxicity: (1) tinnitus or hearing loss (ototoxicity) (2) rising creatinine/decreasing urine output (nephrotoxicity) - vertigo/unsteady gait (vestibulotoxicity) is another accepted answer.
c) Two specific cell types affected: cochlear hair cells and vestibular hair cells (of the inner ear); renal proximal tubular epithelial cells are also affected (nephrotoxicity).
d) One non-biochemical test: audiometry (formal hearing test).
e) Confusion and muscle weakness after starting gentamicin: most likely aminoglycoside-induced neuromuscular blockade (aminoglycosides impair presynaptic acetylcholine release and postsynaptic receptor sensitivity at the neuromuscular junction, mimicking a myasthenic crisis). Treatment: stop the aminoglycoside and administer IV calcium gluconate to reverse the neuromuscular blockade.

D) What are 4 indications for surgical intervention in endocarditis?

cohort_answer.text:
Ampicillin + Gentamicin x 4-6 weeks (4 weeks if symptoms <3 months, 6 weeks if symptoms >3 months or PVE)
Vanco + Gent x 6 weeks
Amp + CTX x 6 weeks (recommended if CrCl <50 at start of therapy or develops on gentamicin)
Indications (1A): Native valve or prosthetic valve IE (Left sided); Valve dysfunction leading to CHF; S aureus, highly antimicrobial resistant organisms (VRE, MDR GNB) or fungal; Abscess/penetrating lesions; Heart block; Persistent bacteremia and/or fever lasting greater than 5-7 days on appropriate therapy. 2A indications: PVE and recurrent bacteremia after clearing cultures; Recurrent emboli with persistent vegetation. 2B indications: Right sided IE - persistent bacteremia or fevers despite effective therapy and large vegetation, or evidence of pulmonary septic emboli; Recurrent emboli on treatment and >10mm mobile vegetation on appropriate treatment

questions.question: Q50 (2008). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Enterococcus endocarditis with questions regarding aminoglycoside resistance testing

parts.text: a) Why do HLAR testing?
b) If susceptible, what does it mean?
c) Mechanism of HLAR in Enterococci

cohort_answer.text: a) Enterococcal endocarditis requires bactericidal regimen but beta-lactams alone aren't readily bactericidal; synergistic bactericidal effect achieved with aminoglycoside addition; synergism = >=2 log10 increase in killing at 24h compared to beta-lactam alone; gentamicin and streptomycin are the two compounds recommended; HLR defined by growth at 2000mg/L streptomycin and 500mg/L gentamicin on BHI agar (or 1000mg/L streptomycin in BHI broth); HLR to both abolishes synergistic effect; evaluation for HLR is standard of care for endovascular/severe enterococcal infections. b) Gentamicin can be used for synergy in endovascular infections. c) Aminoglycoside modifying enzyme (AME) - bifunctional AAC(6')-APH(2'')-Ia confers high level gentamicin resistance due to mutations in 30S ribosomal subunit.

questions.question: Name the most likely mechanism of resistance

parts.text: Serratia marcescens resistant to ertapenem, imipenem AND meropenem, but susceptible to Ceftriaxone
Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to Meropenem, but susceptible to Imipenem
Staphylococcus aureus resistant to daptomycin
Enterococcus gallinarum resistant to vancomycin, but susceptible to teicoplanin
Enterobacter cloacae intermediate to ertapenem, but susceptible to meropenem and cefepime

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). Pseudomonas: RND efflux pump MexAB-OprM (meropenem/doripenem, but not imipenem, are substrates of this efflux system). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. Enterobacter cloacae: Hyperexpression of ampC + porin change combination.

questions.question: 21. Give Gram stain, colony morphology, catalase (if applicable) and rapid bench ID test and result for: a) Group B Strep; b) Enterococcus spp.; c) Candida albicans; d) Proteus vulgaris

b) Enterococcus spp.
c) Candida albicans
d) Proteus vulgaris

cohort_answer.text:
GBS – GPC chains, catalase negative, beta hemolytic, lancefield group B
Enterococcus – GPC pairs/chains, catalase weak positive, alpha or gamma hemolytic, PYR + (GAS too), LAP, bile esculin positive
Candida albicans – "Gram positive" yeast, feet on morphology, germ tube + (also dublinesis), pseudohyphae on wet mount (also with glabrata)
Proteus vulgaris – GNB, catalase +, swarming colony, indole positive, OTC neg (mirabilis +), urease +

parts.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas infections if Septra, Sulfadiazine, and Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra respectively were not available? (give two treatment options each)
A patient with enterococcus infective endocarditis has high level aminoglycoside resistance. What is one issue with using streptomycin?

cohort_answer.text: PJP (no Septra): Severe: Pentamidine 4mg/kg IV, or Clindamycin 450mg PO q6h + Primaquine 15-30mg PO q24h x21d; Mild-moderate: Atovaquone 750mg PO BID with food x21d. Toxoplasma (no Sulfadiazine): Clindamycin 300mg PO q8h + Pyrimethamine, or Atovaquone 750mg PO BID + pyrimethamine. Stenotrophomonas (no Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra): Minocycline 200mg IV x1 then 100mg IV BID, or Levofloxacin 750mg IV/PO q24h, ceftazidime, colistin, cefiderocol. Streptomycin issue: high level resistance = growth in presence of high concentration of streptomycin or gentamicin, meaning no synergistic AG effect possible in vivo if resistant to both; cannot extrapolate resistance of one aminoglycoside based on the other

b) A patient with enterococcus infective endocarditis has high level aminoglycoside resistance. What is one issue with using streptomycin? (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: PJP: 1. Clindamycin-primaquine 2. Atovaquone (mild) or TMP-dapsone (mild) 3. IV pentamidine (severe). Toxoplasma: 1. Pyrimethamine-atovaquone 2. Pyrimethamine-clindamycin 3. Septra or atovaquone. Stenotrophomonas: 1. 2 of: Cefiderocol, minocycline, levofloxacin 2. Ceftazidime-avibactam AND aztreonam. b) Need access to lab for rapid streptomycin level testing; need CrCl >50; lack of familiarity amongst clinicians for streptomycin use; drug availability; high rate of ototoxicity which may not be reversible.

questions.question: Q37 (2014). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. What is the mechanism of resistance in the following scenarios: Serratia (Ertapenem R, Imipenem R, Meropenem R, CFTx S); Pseudomonas (Meropenem R, Imipenem S); E. gallinarum (Vancomycin R); E. cloacae (Cefepime S, Meropenem S, Ceftazidime R, Ertapenem R); MRSA (Daptomycin R); MRSA (Linezolid R)

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each scenario

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Serratia marcescens enzyme (SME) - carbapenemase Class A. Pseudomonas: MexAB-OprM efflux cassette. E. gallinarum: VanC gene presence (chromosomal). E. cloacae: intrinsic resistance to inducible AmpC (R to beta-lactams); OXA-48 (R to Erta, S to Mero with additional efflux pump or porin). MRSA Daptomycin R: mprF gene (phosphatidylglycerol lysyltransferase). MRSA Linezolid R: 23S RNA G2576T point mutation.

questions.question: Q46 (2010 AM, 2009 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance (fill in the blank table): K. pneumoniae with Meropenem; P. aeruginosa with Meropenem; E faecium with penicillin; E faecalis with high level aminoglycoside resistance; S. pneumoniae with moxifloxacin; S. pyogenes with erythromycin

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair

cohort_answer.text: K. pneumoniae/Meropenem: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A KPCs; reduced expression of OmpK35/OmpK36. P. aeruginosa/Meropenem: downregulated/absent OprD porin with background AmpC; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM-1 less common); upregulation of MexA-MexB-OprM efflux (resistant to mero/doripenem but not imipenem). E. faecium/Penicillin: altered PBPs (resistant pbp5 allele). E. faecalis/HLAR: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2'')-Ia. S. pneumoniae/Moxifloxacin: dual mutations in GyrA and ParC. S. pyogenes/Erythromycin: erm gene (ribosome methylation) - methylase enzymes dimethylate adenine on 23S rRNA of 50S subunit, disrupting MLS binding.

questions.question: Q54 (2006 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. A) E. faecium with MIC >256 for both teicoplanin and vancomycin. B) Salmonella enteritidis (resistance stem unclear). C) Enterobacter cloacae resistant to cephalosporins

parts.text: A) Mechanism for E. faecium high-level vanco/teicoplanin resistance
B) Salmonella enteritidis resistance mechanism
C) E. cloacae cephalosporin resistance mechanism

cohort_answer.text: A) VanA gene acquisition - mediates high level vanco resistance by target modification to D-ala-D-lac; most common type, usually higher level resistance, cross-resistance to teicoplanin. B) Incompatible (Inc) plasmids - IncH1 plasmid acquisition leads to concurrent resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, TMP/SMX. C) Class C - AmpC beta-lactamase (chromosomal).
